courses.title: Law of Contract I: General Principles, LLB Semester 1
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: Offer, acceptance and communication
topics.summary: Proposal, acceptance, communication and revocation under the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
notes: A proposal (section 2(a)) becomes a promise when accepted (2(b)); an agreement enforceable by law is a contract (2(h)).
An invitation to treat (display of goods, advertisements, auction calls) is not an offer (Pharmaceutical Society v Boots; Harvey v Facey).
A general offer can be accepted by anyone performing its conditions (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.; Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt: knowledge of the offer is needed).
Communication of acceptance is complete against the proposer when posted, and against the acceptor when it reaches the proposer (section 4).
outcomes: Distinguish offers from invitations to treat
Decide when a contract is concluded by post or electronically

lesson.hook: A shop tags a TV at ₹1,000 by mistake. Can a customer insist on buying it at that price?

questions.q: Is a price list an offer?
questions.a: No, it is an invitation to treat.

questions.q: When is acceptance by post complete against the proposer?
questions.a: When the letter of acceptance is posted, putting it out of the acceptor's power.

topics.title: Consideration and competence to contract
topics.summary: Consideration, privity, and minors and persons of unsound mind.
notes: Consideration may move from the promisee or any other person (section 2(d); Chinnaya v Ramayya).
An agreement without consideration is void except as section 25 allows (natural love and affection in writing and registered, past voluntary service, promise to pay a time-barred debt in writing).
A minor's agreement is void ab initio (Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose, 1903); no estoppel against a minor.
Persons of unsound mind cannot contract while unsound (section 12).

topics.title: Coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation and mistake
topics.summary: Factors vitiating consent and their effect.
notes: Consent is free unless caused by coercion (15), undue influence (16), fraud (17), misrepresentation (18) or mistake (20–22).
Coercion, undue influence, fraud and misrepresentation make the contract voidable (sections 19, 19A).
A bilateral mistake of fact essential to the agreement makes it void (section 20); a mistake of Indian law does not (section 21).
outcomes: State the effect on the contract

topics.title: Void agreements and discharge
topics.summary: Unlawful objects, restraint of trade, wagers and frustration.
notes: Agreements in restraint of trade are void (section 27) except sale of goodwill; post-employment restraints are void in India.
Wagering agreements are void (section 30).
Frustration: a contract becomes void when performance becomes impossible or unlawful (section 56; Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur).

topics.title: Breach and remedies
topics.summary: Damages, quasi-contracts and specific relief.
notes: Damages for loss arising naturally or within the parties' contemplation (section 73; Hadley v Baxendale); remote losses are not recoverable.
Liquidated damages and penalties: reasonable compensation up to the stated sum (section 74).
Quasi-contracts (sections 68–72): e.g. payment by mistake must be repaid (section 72).
After the 2018 amendment of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance is the general rule, not discretionary.

courses.title: Constitutional Law I, LLB Semester 1
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: Salient features and the Preamble
topics.summary: Making of the Constitution, its features and the Preamble.
notes: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.
Features: written, federal with a strong centre, parliamentary government, fundamental rights, independent judiciary, rigid and flexible amendment.
The Preamble is part of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973); "socialist", "secular" and "integrity" were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
outcomes: Discuss the status of the Preamble

topics.title: Articles 12–18
topics.summary: State, judicial review, equality and reservation.
notes: "State" under Article 12 includes instrumentalities of the State (Ajay Hasia; Pradeep Kumar Biswas).
Article 14 permits reasonable classification (intelligible differentia with a rational nexus) and forbids arbitrariness (E. P. Royappa).
Indra Sawhney (1992): 50% ceiling on reservation, creamy layer exclusion; Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld the EWS quota.
outcomes: Apply the test of reasonable classification

topics.title: Articles 19–22
topics.summary: Freedoms, protections in criminal matters and right to life.
notes: Article 19(1) freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions in 19(2)–(6).
Article 20: no ex post facto criminal law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination.
Article 21: procedure must be fair, just and reasonable (Maneka Gandhi, 1978); privacy is a fundamental right (K. S. Puttaswamy, 2017).
Article 22: an arrested person must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.

lesson.hook: Can the government seize your passport without telling you why?

questions.q: Which case held that the procedure under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable?
questions.a: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978).

questions.q: Which case recognised privacy as a fundamental right?
questions.a: Justice K. S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017).

topics.title: Constitutional remedies, directive principles and duties
topics.summary: Writs, Article 32 and 226, DPSPs and fundamental duties.
notes: Article 32 is a fundamental right to move the Supreme Court; High Courts issue writs under Article 226 (wider: "for any other purpose").
Writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto.
DPSPs (Part IV) are not enforceable but fundamental in governance; harmony with fundamental rights is a basic feature (Minerva Mills, 1980).
Fundamental duties (Article 51A) were added by the 42nd Amendment.

courses.title: Law of Torts, Motor Vehicles Act and Consumer Protection, LLB Semester 1
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: Nature of tort
topics.summary: Definition, elements and maxims.
notes: A tort is a civil wrong, other than breach of contract or trust, remedied by unliquidated damages.
Injuria sine damno is actionable (Ashby v White); damnum sine injuria is not (Gloucester Grammar School case).
General defences: volenti non fit injuria, inevitable accident, act of God, private defence, necessity, statutory authority.
outcomes: Identify the elements of a tort

topics.title: Negligence
topics.summary: Duty of care, breach, causation and damage.
notes: Duty of care: neighbour principle (Donoghue v Stevenson, 1932).
Breach is judged by the reasonable person standard; res ipsa loquitur infers negligence from the facts.
Medical negligence: the Bolam test as applied in Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab (2005).

topics.title: Strict and absolute liability, nuisance and defamation
topics.summary: Rylands v Fletcher, absolute liability and other torts.
notes: Strict liability (Rylands v Fletcher, 1868) for escape of dangerous things, with exceptions.
Absolute liability for hazardous industries, with no exceptions (M. C. Mehta v Union of India, 1987, the Oleum gas case).
Defamation: libel (permanent form) and slander (transient); defences are truth, fair comment and privilege.

topics.title: Vicarious liability
topics.summary: Master and servant, and liability of the State.
notes: An employer is liable for torts of employees in the course of employment.
State liability: sovereign functions (Kasturilal, 1965) narrowed by later cases awarding compensation for violation of fundamental rights (Rudul Sah; Nilabati Behera).
Constitutional tort: compensation under Articles 32 and 226.
outcomes: Decide when an employer is vicariously liable

topics.title: Motor accident claims and consumer protection
topics.summary: MV Act claims and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
notes: Claims tribunals (MACT) decide motor accident compensation; no-fault liability is ₹5 lakh for death and ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt (section 164).
Compensation by the multiplier method (Sarla Verma; Pranay Sethi).
Consumer Protection Act, 2019: consumer rights, product liability, unfair trade practices, e-commerce; district, state and national commissions.
outcomes: Compute compensation by the multiplier method
File a consumer complaint in the right forum

courses.title: Family Law I: Hindu Law, LLB Semester 1
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: Sources and schools of Hindu law
topics.summary: Sources, schools and who is a Hindu.
notes: Sources: Shruti, Smriti, commentaries and digests, custom, legislation and judicial decisions.
Schools: Mitakshara and Dayabhaga.
The codified Acts apply to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs.

topics.title: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
topics.summary: Conditions of marriage, void and voidable marriages, and matrimonial remedies.
notes: Conditions (section 5): monogamy, sound mind, age 21 (groom) and 18 (bride), not within prohibited degrees or sapindas (unless custom permits).
Saptapadi completes the marriage where it is the essential ceremony (section 7).

Divorce grounds (section 13) include cruelty, desertion for two years, conversion and mental disorder; divorce by mutual consent under section 13B (the six-month period may be waived: Amardeep Singh, 2017).
The Supreme Court can grant divorce for irretrievable breakdown under Article 142 (Shilpa Sailesh, 2023).
outcomes: Test the validity of a Hindu marriage

topics.title: HAMA and HMGA
topics.summary: Adoption, maintenance and guardianship under the 1956 Acts.
notes: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956: who may adopt and be adopted; a single woman may adopt.
Wife, children and aged parents are entitled to maintenance; also BNSS section 144 (formerly CrPC 125) for all communities.
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956: welfare of the minor is paramount; the mother can be natural guardian (Githa Hariharan, 1999).
outcomes: State the rules of valid adoption

topics.title: Hindu Succession Act, 1956
topics.summary: Coparcenary, intestate succession and the 2005 amendment.
notes: Since the 2005 amendment, a daughter is a coparcener by birth (section 6); applies regardless of whether the father was alive in 2005 (Vineeta Sharma, 2020).
Class I heirs (son, daughter, widow, mother and others) take simultaneously and equally.
A Hindu female's property is her absolute property (section 14).
outcomes: Distribute an intestate Hindu male's property

courses.title: Criminal Law I: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, LLB Semester 1
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: Crime and its elements
topics.summary: Actus reus, mens rea and stages of crime.
notes: Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea: the act is not guilty unless the mind is guilty.
Stages: intention, preparation, attempt (punishable, section 62), commission.
Joint liability: common intention (section 3(5)) and common object of an unlawful assembly (section 190).
outcomes: Identify actus reus and mens rea

topics.title: General exceptions and private defence
topics.summary: Mistake, accident, infancy, insanity, intoxication and private defence.
notes: Nothing is an offence by a child under 7 (section 20); a child of 7–12 lacking maturity of understanding is also exempt (section 21).
Insanity (section 22) follows the M'Naghten rules: incapacity to know the nature of the act or that it is wrong.
Private defence (sections 34–44) extends to causing death in cases listed in sections 38 (body) and 41 (property).
outcomes: Decide the limits of private defence

topics.title: Culpable homicide and murder
topics.summary: Distinguishing culpable homicide from murder and their punishments.
notes: Culpable homicide (section 100); murder (section 101) with exceptions such as grave and sudden provocation and exceeding private defence.
Murder is punished under section 103; murder by a group of five or more on grounds such as race, caste or religion (mob lynching) is punishable under section 103(2).
Reg v Govinda guides the distinction between culpable homicide and murder.

lesson.hook: Two men fight; one dies after a single blow to the head. Murder, culpable homicide, or neither?

questions.q: Name one exception that reduces murder to culpable homicide.
questions.a: Grave and sudden provocation (others: private defence exceeded in good faith, sudden fight, consent).

chapters.title: Offences against Property and New Offences

topics.title: Theft, extortion, robbery, cheating and organised crime
topics.summary: Property offences and offences new in the BNS.
notes: Theft (section 303) needs dishonest intention, movable property, without consent, and moving it; snatching is a separate offence (section 304).
Robbery (section 309) is theft or extortion with violence; dacoity (section 310) is robbery by five or more.
Cheating (section 318) and criminal breach of trust (section 316).
New offences: organised crime (section 111), petty organised crime (112), terrorist act (113).
outcomes: Distinguish theft, extortion, robbery and dacoity
Identify the new offences in the BNS

courses.title: Law of Contract II: Special Contracts, LLB Semester 2
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: Indemnity and guarantee
topics.summary: Contracts of indemnity and guarantee and the surety's rights.
notes: Indemnity (section 124): a promise to save another from loss.
Guarantee (section 126): three parties — creditor, principal debtor, surety; the surety's liability is co-extensive with the debtor's (section 128).
The surety is discharged by variance in terms, release of the principal debtor, or the creditor's act impairing the surety's remedy.
outcomes: Identify when a surety is discharged

topics.title: Bailment and pledge
topics.summary: Duties of bailor and bailee and pledge.
notes: Bailment (section 148): delivery of goods for a purpose, to be returned.
The bailee must take the care a person of ordinary prudence takes of his own goods (section 151).
Pledge (section 172) is bailment as security for a debt; the pawnee may sell after reasonable notice.
outcomes: State the duties of a bailee

topics.title: Contract of agency
topics.summary: Creation, authority and termination of agency.
notes: An agent is employed to act for another in dealings with third persons (section 182).
Agency by express or implied authority, ratification, necessity, or estoppel.
Agency coupled with an interest cannot be revoked to the agent's prejudice (section 202).
outcomes: Decide the principal's liability for an agent's acts

topics.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 and Partnership Act, 1932
topics.summary: Conditions and warranties, transfer of property, and partnership.
notes: Implied conditions: title, description, quality or fitness, sample.
Nemo dat quod non habet: no one gives what he does not have, with exceptions.
Partnership (section 4): agreement to share profits of a business carried on by all or any acting for all; partners are jointly and severally liable.
LLP Act, 2008 gives limited liability with partnership flexibility.

courses.title: Constitutional Law II, LLB Semester 2
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: President, Governor and Council of Ministers
topics.summary: Executive powers and the parliamentary system.
notes: The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74; Shamsher Singh, 1974).
Ordinance power (Article 123) is subject to judicial review (Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017).
Pardoning power: President (Article 72) and Governor (Article 161).

topics.title: Parliament and legislative procedure
topics.summary: Composition, privileges and law-making.
notes: Money bills (Article 110) can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days.
Anti-defection law: Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985).
Parliamentary privileges (Article 105).
outcomes: Trace the passage of a bill

topics.title: Supreme Court and High Courts
topics.summary: Jurisdiction, independence and appointments.
notes: Jurisdictions of the Supreme Court: original (Article 131), appellate (132–136), advisory (143).
Special leave petition (Article 136) is discretionary.
Collegium system (Second and Third Judges cases); the NJAC was struck down (2015).

topics.title: Centre–State relations, emergencies and amendment
topics.summary: Distribution of powers, emergencies and Article 368.
notes: Seventh Schedule: Union, State and Concurrent Lists; residuary power with the Union (Article 248).
Emergencies: national (352), State (356, President's rule; S. R. Bommai, 1994), financial (360).
Basic structure doctrine limits amending power (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).
outcomes: Resolve conflicts between Union and State laws

courses.title: Family Law II: Muslim Law and Other Personal Laws, LLB Semester 2
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: Sources and nikah
topics.summary: Sources of Muslim law, schools and marriage.
notes: Sources: Quran, Sunna, Ijma, Qiyas; schools: Sunni (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) and Shia.
Nikah is a contract; essentials: offer and acceptance, competence, witnesses (Sunni law).
Mahr (dower) is the wife's right: prompt or deferred.
outcomes: State the essentials of a valid nikah

topics.title: Talaq and other modes
topics.summary: Forms of talaq and the statutory position.
notes: Talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq) was held invalid (Shayara Bano, 2017) and made an offence by the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.
Talaq-e-ahsan and hasan; khula (at the wife's instance) and mubarat (mutual).
Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 gives the wife judicial grounds.
outcomes: State the wife's grounds for divorce

topics.title: Maintenance and succession
topics.summary: Maintenance of divorced women and inheritance rules.
notes: Shah Bano (1985) and Danial Latifi (2001): reasonable and fair provision for a divorced wife.
Divorced Muslim women can also claim maintenance under BNSS section 144 (Mohd. Abdul Samad, 2024).
Inheritance: sharers, residuaries and distant kindred; a bequest is limited to one-third of the estate.
outcomes: Apply the one-third rule on wills

topics.title: Christian, Parsi and secular laws
topics.summary: Indian Succession Act, Special Marriage Act and the uniform civil code debate.
notes: Indian Succession Act, 1925 governs Christian (and testamentary) succession.
Special Marriage Act, 1954 provides a civil marriage for any two persons, with 30 days' notice.
Article 44 directs the State to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code; Uttarakhand enacted one in 2024.

courses.title: Environmental Law, LLB Semester 2
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: Environment and the Constitution
topics.summary: Articles 21, 48A and 51A(g), and public interest litigation.
notes: Right to a healthy environment is part of Article 21 (Subhash Kumar, 1991).
Article 48A (State duty) and 51A(g) (citizens' duty) protect the environment.
PIL widened access to courts in environmental matters (M. C. Mehta cases).
outcomes: Explain the constitutional basis of environmental rights

topics.title: Environmental principles
topics.summary: Sustainable development, precautionary, polluter pays and public trust.
notes: Precautionary and polluter pays principles are part of Indian law (Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum, 1996).
Public trust doctrine: the State holds natural resources in trust (M. C. Mehta v Kamal Nath, 1997).
Inter-generational equity and sustainable development balance growth and environment.

topics.title: Water, Air and Environment Protection Acts
topics.summary: Pollution control boards and the EPA, 1986.
notes: Water Act, 1974 and Air Act, 1981 created the Central and State Pollution Control Boards; consent to establish and operate is required.
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is an umbrella law; EIA Notification, 2006 requires prior environmental clearance.
Hazardous wastes, plastic waste and e-waste are governed by rules under the EPA.

topics.title: Forest and wildlife laws and the National Green Tribunal
topics.summary: Forest (Conservation) Act, Wild Life Act and NGT.
notes: Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 (renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam in 2023) needs approval for diverting forest land.
Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 lists protected species in schedules and creates protected areas.
NGT Act, 2010: the Tribunal decides environmental cases on the principles of sustainable development, precaution and polluter pays.

courses.title: Jurisprudence, LLB Semester 3
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Natural law and positivism
topics.summary: Natural law and the analytical school.
notes: Natural law: law derives from reason or morality (Aquinas; modern: Fuller's inner morality of law).
Austin: law is the command of the sovereign backed by sanction.
Hart: law is a union of primary rules (duties) and secondary rules (recognition, change, adjudication).
Kelsen's pure theory: a hierarchy of norms resting on the grundnorm.

topics.title: Historical, sociological and realist schools
topics.summary: Savigny, Pound and legal realism.
notes: Savigny: law grows from the Volksgeist (spirit of the people).
Pound: law as social engineering balancing interests.
Realists (Holmes, Llewellyn): law is what courts actually do.

topics.title: Legislation, precedent and custom
topics.summary: Sources of law and the doctrine of precedent.
notes: Precedent: ratio decidendi binds; obiter dicta persuade; Article 141 binds all courts by the Supreme Court's law.
A valid custom must be ancient, certain, reasonable and continuous.
Delegated legislation must stay within the parent Act.
outcomes: Test the validity of a custom

topics.title: Rights, duties and legal personality
topics.summary: Hohfeld's analysis, possession, ownership and persons.
notes: Hohfeld's jural correlatives: right–duty, privilege–no-right, power–liability, immunity–disability.
Possession has corpus (control) and animus (intention).
Legal persons include corporations, idols (Ram Janmabhoomi case) and, by some courts, rivers.

courses.title: Property Law (Transfer of Property Act, 1882), LLB Semester 3
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: Transfer of property
topics.summary: Definition, transferable interests and conditions.
notes: Transfer of property (section 5) is an act by which a living person conveys property to others.
Not transferable (section 6) include spes successionis, mere right to sue, and public offices.
Conditions absolutely restraining alienation are void (section 10); rule against perpetuity (section 14).

topics.title: Doctrines protecting transferees
topics.summary: Ostensible owner, part performance and lis pendens.
notes: Transfer by ostensible owner (section 41) protects a bona fide purchaser.
Lis pendens (section 52): property in litigation cannot be transferred to affect the parties' rights.
Part performance (section 53A) protects a transferee in possession under a written contract.
outcomes: Advise a purchaser of disputed property

topics.title: Sale and mortgages
topics.summary: Sale of immovable property and kinds of mortgage.
notes: Sale of tangible immovable property worth ₹100 or more must be by registered instrument (section 54).
A contract for sale creates no interest in the property.
Mortgages (section 58): simple, by conditional sale, usufructuary, English, by deposit of title deeds, anomalous; right of redemption (section 60).
outcomes: Distinguish sale and contract for sale

topics.title: Lease, gift and easements
topics.summary: Leases, gifts and easementary rights.
notes: Lease (section 105): transfer of a right to enjoy property for a term for a price.
Gift (section 122) of immovable property must be by registered instrument, accepted during the donor's lifetime.
Easements Act, 1882: easement by prescription after 20 years' peaceable and open enjoyment.
outcomes: Advise on creating a lease or gift

courses.title: Administrative Law, LLB Semester 3
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Rule of law and separation of powers
topics.summary: Dicey's rule of law and separation of powers in India.
notes: Dicey: supremacy of law, equality before law, constitution as the result of ordinary law.
India has functional separation of powers (Ram Jawaya Kapur, 1955); judicial review is a basic feature.
Administrative law governs the powers and procedures of administrative authorities.
outcomes: Discuss separation of powers in India

topics.title: Delegated legislation and its control
topics.summary: Reasons, limits and parliamentary and judicial control.
notes: Essential legislative functions cannot be delegated (In re Delhi Laws Act, 1951).
Controls: parliamentary (laying), judicial (ultra vires), procedural (publication, consultation).
Sub-delegation needs authority in the parent Act.
outcomes: Test the validity of delegated legislation

topics.title: Principles of natural justice
topics.summary: Rule against bias and the right to a hearing.
notes: Nemo judex in causa sua: no one should be a judge in his own cause (A. K. Kraipak, 1969).
Audi alteram partem: hear the other side; notice and opportunity (Maneka Gandhi).
Exceptions: emergency, confidentiality, legislative action; reasoned decisions are required.

topics.title: Judicial review of administrative action
topics.summary: Grounds of review, writs and other remedies.
notes: Grounds (CCSU case): illegality, irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness), procedural impropriety; proportionality in rights cases.
Legitimate expectation protects reasonable expectations from arbitrary change.
Other remedies: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; RTI Act, 2005; tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B.
outcomes: Choose a remedy against administrative action

courses.title: Labour and Industrial Law, LLB Semester 3
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2024-25)

topics.title: Industry, workman and industrial disputes
topics.summary: Key definitions and dispute resolution.
notes: "Industry" was defined broadly by the triple test in Bangalore Water Supply v A. Rajappa (1978).
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 consolidates the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Trade Unions Act, 1926 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946.
Dispute resolution machinery: grievance redressal committee, conciliation, tribunals, arbitration.

topics.title: Strikes, lockouts and retrenchment
topics.summary: Conditions for strikes and protection against job loss.
notes: Under the IR Code, 14 days' notice is required before a strike or lockout in any establishment.
Retrenchment compensation is 15 days' average pay for every completed year of service; "last in, first out" applies.
Prior government permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure applies to establishments with 300 or more workers.
outcomes: State the conditions for a lawful strike

topics.title: Code on Wages and Code on Social Security
topics.summary: Minimum wages, payment of wages, bonus and social security.
notes: The Code on Wages, 2019 introduces a national floor wage and covers minimum wages, payment of wages, bonus and equal remuneration.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 covers EPF, ESI, gratuity, maternity benefit and gig and platform workers.
Gratuity is payable after five years' continuous service at 15 days' wages per year (fixed-term employees after one year).
outcomes: Explain coverage of wage and social security laws

topics.title: Occupational safety, health and working conditions
topics.summary: OSH Code, working hours and welfare.
notes: The OSH Code, 2020 consolidates the Factories Act, Mines Act and others.
Daily working hours are capped at 8 hours (weekly 48), with overtime at twice the wage rate.
Welfare provisions: canteens, crèches, first aid, safety committees.

courses.title: Public International Law, LLB Semester 4
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Nature and sources of international law
topics.summary: Whether international law is law, and its sources.
notes: Sources (Article 38(1), ICJ Statute): treaties, custom, general principles of law; judicial decisions and teachings as subsidiary means.
Custom needs state practice and opinio juris (North Sea Continental Shelf, 1969).
Jus cogens norms (e.g. prohibition of genocide, torture) cannot be derogated from.

topics.title: Statehood, recognition and jurisdiction
topics.summary: Criteria of statehood, recognition theories and state jurisdiction.
notes: Montevideo Convention criteria: population, territory, government, capacity to enter relations.
Recognition: constitutive and declaratory theories; de jure and de facto.
Jurisdiction principles: territorial, nationality, protective, universal.

topics.title: Law of treaties and law of the sea
topics.summary: Vienna Convention, 1969 and UNCLOS, 1982.
notes: Pacta sunt servanda (Article 26, VCLT); reservations; rebus sic stantibus (fundamental change of circumstances).
UNCLOS zones: territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles, contiguous zone 24, exclusive economic zone 200.
Innocent passage is allowed through the territorial sea.

topics.title: The United Nations and the ICJ
topics.summary: UN organs, peaceful settlement and use of force.
notes: Principal UN organs: General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council, ICJ, Secretariat.
Article 2(4) of the UN Charter prohibits the use of force; exceptions are self-defence (Article 51) and Security Council action (Chapter VII).
ICJ jurisdiction rests on consent (special agreement, compromissory clause, optional clause).
outcomes: Explain the prohibition on the use of force
Describe how the ICJ gets jurisdiction

courses.title: Company Law, LLB Semester 4
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Incorporation and lifting the veil
topics.summary: Separate legal personality and when courts pierce it.
notes: A company is a separate legal person (Salomon v Salomon, 1897).
The veil is lifted for fraud, sham companies, tax evasion and enemy character; section 7(7) and others allow statutory lifting.
Kinds: private, public, OPC, small, Section 8 (charitable), producer companies.
outcomes: Identify when the veil is lifted

topics.title: MOA, AOA and share capital
topics.summary: Constitutional documents, doctrines and capital.
notes: Ultra vires acts are void (Ashbury Railway Carriage v Riche, 1875).
Indoor management (Royal British Bank v Turquand) protects outsiders; constructive notice applies to public documents.
Share capital: equity and preference; buy-back (section 68); reduction of capital (section 66).
outcomes: Apply ultra vires and indoor management

topics.title: Directors, meetings and governance
topics.summary: Directors' duties, meetings and minority protection.
notes: Directors' duties (section 166): act in good faith, with due care, avoid conflicts.
Oppression and mismanagement remedies (sections 241–244) before the NCLT; class actions (section 245).
Related party transactions (section 188) need approval.

topics.title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
topics.summary: Corporate insolvency resolution and liquidation.
notes: CIRP starts on default of at least ₹1 crore; financial or operational creditors may apply to the NCLT.
A resolution professional runs the company; the committee of creditors approves a resolution plan by 66% vote.
Timeline: 180 days, extendable by 90, with an outer limit of 330 days.

courses.title: Law of Evidence (Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023), LLB Semester 4
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Facts in issue and relevant facts
topics.summary: Relevancy, res gestae and motive.
notes: Evidence may be given only of facts in issue and relevant facts.
Res gestae: facts forming part of the same transaction are relevant (section 4).
Motive, preparation and conduct are relevant (section 6).
outcomes: Distinguish facts in issue and relevant facts

topics.title: Admissions, confessions and dying declarations
topics.summary: When statements are admissible against their makers.
notes: A confession to a police officer is not provable (section 23); a confession under inducement, threat or promise is irrelevant (section 22).
Information leading to the discovery of a fact is admissible (proviso to section 23, formerly section 27).
A dying declaration as to the cause of death is relevant (section 26(a)); it can alone support conviction if reliable.

lesson.hook: An accused tells police, "I threw the knife in the well." The knife is found there. What can the court hear?

questions.q: Is a confession made to a police officer admissible?
questions.a: No (section 23), except the part that leads to discovery of a fact.

topics.title: Documents and electronic records
topics.summary: Primary and secondary evidence and electronic records.
notes: Primary evidence is the document itself; secondary evidence is admissible in listed cases.
Electronic records are documents and can be primary evidence (sections 57, 61).
A certificate under section 63 (formerly 65B; Arjun Panditrao Khotkar, 2020) is needed for electronic records as secondary evidence.

topics.title: Burden, presumptions and examination of witnesses
topics.summary: Who must prove, presumptions, and examination-in-chief and cross-examination.
notes: Burden of proof lies on the person who asserts (section 104).
Presumptions: "may presume", "shall presume", "conclusive proof".
Leading questions are not allowed in examination-in-chief but are allowed in cross-examination.

courses.title: Intellectual Property Rights Law, LLB Semester 4
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Nature of IP and international framework
topics.summary: Kinds of IP and TRIPS.
notes: IP rights: copyright, patents, trademarks, designs, geographical indications, trade secrets.
TRIPS Agreement (WTO) sets minimum standards.
IP rights are territorial and time-limited (except trademarks, renewable).

topics.title: Patents Act, 1970
topics.summary: Patentability, exclusions and term.
notes: Patentable invention: novelty, inventive step, industrial application.
Section 3(d) bars new forms of known substances without enhanced efficacy (Novartis v Union of India, 2013).
Term: 20 years from filing; compulsory licences (section 84).

topics.title: Copyright Act, 1957
topics.summary: Works, rights, term and fair dealing.
notes: Protects original literary, dramatic, musical, artistic works, films and sound recordings.
Term: author's life plus 60 years for literary works.
Fair dealing for private use, research, criticism and reporting (section 52).

topics.title: Trade Marks Act, 1999 and Designs Act, 2000
topics.summary: Registration, infringement and passing off.
notes: A trademark must be capable of distinguishing goods or services; registration lasts 10 years, renewable.
Infringement for registered marks; passing off protects unregistered goodwill.
Design registration lasts 10 years, extendable by 5.

courses.title: Civil Procedure Code and Limitation Act, LLB Semester 5
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Jurisdiction and bars to suits
topics.summary: Civil jurisdiction, res sub judice and res judicata.
notes: Civil courts try all suits of a civil nature unless barred (section 9).
Res sub judice (section 10) stays a later suit on the same matter; res judicata (section 11) bars re-litigation of decided matters.
Place of suing (sections 15–20): the lowest competent court; where the defendant resides or the cause of action arises.

topics.title: Plaint, written statement and interim orders
topics.summary: Pleadings, appearance and interim relief.
notes: Plaint (Order VII); rejection of plaint (Order VII Rule 11).
Written statement within 30 days, extendable to 90 days (120 days, non-extendable, in commercial suits).
Temporary injunctions (Order XXXIX Rules 1–2) need a prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable injury.
outcomes: Draft the structure of a plaint
Apply the test for temporary injunction

topics.title: Decree, appeal, review, revision and execution
topics.summary: Post-trial remedies.
notes: Decree (section 2(2)); first appeal (section 96); second appeal on a substantial question of law (section 100).
Review (section 114, Order XLVII); revision (section 115); inherent powers (section 151).
Execution of decrees by the court that passed it or to which it is sent (section 38).

topics.title: Limitation Act, 1963
topics.summary: Bar of limitation, extension and computation.
notes: A suit filed after the limitation period is dismissed even if limitation is not pleaded (section 3).
Condonation of delay for appeals and applications on sufficient cause (section 5); not for suits.
Common periods: suit on contract 3 years; residuary 3 years (Article 113); possession of immovable property based on title 12 years.

courses.title: Criminal Procedure (Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023), LLB Semester 5
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: FIR, investigation and arrest
topics.summary: Information to police, investigation and arrest powers.
notes: FIR for cognizable offences (section 173); e-FIR and zero FIR are recognised.
Preliminary enquiry is allowed for offences punishable with 3 to 7 years (section 173(3)).
Arrest without warrant (section 35); notice of appearance instead of arrest in suitable cases; arrest memo and informing relatives (D. K. Basu guidelines).

topics.title: Remand and bail
topics.summary: Police and judicial custody, default bail and anticipatory bail.
notes: Police custody up to 15 days in total, which may be taken in parts within the first 40 or 60 days (section 187).
Default bail if the charge-sheet is not filed within 60 or 90 days.
Bailable and non-bailable offences; anticipatory bail (section 482); "bail is the rule, jail the exception".
outcomes: Compute remand and default bail periods

topics.title: Charges and trials
topics.summary: Charge, trial procedures and plea bargaining.
notes: Trials: sessions, warrant, summons and summary trials.
Plea bargaining (Chapter XXIII) is available for offences punishable up to 7 years, except specified offences.
Trial in absentia of proclaimed offenders is now possible in specified cases.
outcomes: Identify the trial procedure for an offence

topics.title: Appeals, revision and maintenance
topics.summary: Post-trial remedies and miscellaneous proceedings.
notes: Appeals against conviction and acquittal; revision by Sessions Courts and High Courts.
Maintenance of wives, children and parents (section 144).
Victim compensation scheme (section 396).
outcomes: Advise on maintenance and victim compensation

courses.title: Interpretation of Statutes, LLB Semester 5
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Literal, golden and mischief rules
topics.summary: Primary rules of statutory interpretation.
notes: Literal rule: plain meaning of words.
Golden rule: modify literal meaning to avoid absurdity.
Mischief rule (Heydon's case, 1584): find the mischief the law was meant to remedy; purposive interpretation is its modern form.
outcomes: Apply the three rules to a statute
Choose an approach for an ambiguous provision

topics.title: Maxims of interpretation
topics.summary: Ejusdem generis, noscitur a sociis and others.
notes: Ejusdem generis: general words following specific ones take their colour.
Noscitur a sociis: a word is known by its companions.
Expressio unius est exclusio alterius: express mention of one excludes others.
outcomes: Interpret general words in a list

topics.title: Internal and external aids
topics.summary: Preamble, headings, definitions and legislative history.
notes: Internal aids: title, preamble, headings, definitions, provisos, explanations, schedules.
External aids: parliamentary debates, committee reports, dictionaries, earlier statutes.
General Clauses Act, 1897 supplies common definitions and rules.

topics.title: Penal, taxing and beneficial statutes
topics.summary: Strict and liberal construction.
notes: Penal and taxing statutes are construed strictly in favour of the subject.
Beneficial and welfare legislation is construed liberally.
Presumption of constitutionality; reading down to save a statute.

courses.title: Professional Ethics and Accounting for Lawyers (Clinical), LLB Semester 5
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Advocates Act, 1961
topics.summary: Enrolment, Bar Councils and rights of advocates.
notes: State Bar Councils enrol advocates; the Bar Council of India sets standards and the All India Bar Examination.
Only enrolled advocates may practise in courts (section 30).
Misconduct leads to disciplinary proceedings (section 35).

topics.title: BCI Rules on professional conduct
topics.summary: Duties to court, client, opponent and colleagues.
notes: Duties to the court: act with dignity, not influence the court by illegal means.
Duties to the client: not withdraw without sufficient cause, keep confidences, avoid conflicts.
Advertising and solicitation are prohibited (Rule 36).
outcomes: Apply the BCI Rules to cases

topics.title: Contempt of court
topics.summary: Civil and criminal contempt and defences.
notes: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971: civil (wilful disobedience) and criminal (scandalising, prejudicing proceedings).
Truth is a defence if in the public interest and bona fide (2006 amendment).
Mutual respect between bar and bench sustains justice.

topics.title: Accountancy for lawyers
topics.summary: Client money, books of account and fees.
notes: Advocates must keep accounts of clients' money separately.
Fees cannot be contingent on the result (no share in the subject matter).
Receipts and statements of account must be given to clients.

courses.title: Alternative Dispute Resolution (Clinical), LLB Semester 6
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Forms of ADR
topics.summary: Arbitration, conciliation, mediation, negotiation and Lok Adalats.
notes: Section 89 CPC lets courts refer disputes to ADR.
Negotiation and mediation are non-binding until settled; arbitration gives a binding award.
ADR is quicker, cheaper and confidential.

topics.title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
topics.summary: Arbitration agreement, tribunal, award and challenge.
notes: An arbitration agreement must be in writing (section 7); courts refer parties to arbitration (section 8).
Appointment of arbitrators (section 11); the tribunal rules on its own jurisdiction (section 16, kompetenz-kompetenz).
Award within 12 months of completion of pleadings, extendable by 6 months (section 29A); set aside under section 34; enforced under section 36.
outcomes: State grounds to set aside an award

topics.title: Mediation Act, 2023
topics.summary: Pre-litigation mediation and mediated settlement agreements.
notes: Mediation is voluntary; a mediated settlement agreement is final and enforceable like a court judgment.
Mediation should be completed within 120 days, extendable by 60.
Online mediation is recognised.

topics.title: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
topics.summary: Lok Adalats and free legal aid.
notes: A Lok Adalat award is deemed a civil court decree and final; no appeal lies.
Permanent Lok Adalats handle public utility services disputes.
Free legal aid is a right under Article 39A and Article 21 (Hussainara Khatoon).
outcomes: Identify who is entitled to legal aid

courses.title: Drafting, Pleading and Conveyancing (Clinical), LLB Semester 6
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: General principles
topics.summary: Clarity, precision and structure in legal drafting.
notes: Use plain, precise language; define terms; avoid ambiguity.
Structure: title, parties, recitals, operative part, schedules, execution.
Stamp duty and registration requirements affect validity and admissibility.

topics.title: Plaint and written statement
topics.summary: Drafting civil pleadings.
notes: Order VI: pleadings state material facts, not evidence or law.
A plaint states the court, parties, cause of action, jurisdiction, valuation, relief and verification.
A written statement must deny specifically; non-denial is admission (Order VIII Rule 5).
outcomes: Draft a plaint for recovery of money

topics.title: Complaints, bail and petitions
topics.summary: Drafting in criminal matters.
notes: Private complaint to a magistrate (BNSS section 223).
Bail applications state grounds: nature of offence, antecedents, custody period, cooperation.
Writ petitions under Article 226: facts, grounds, prayer, affidavit.

topics.title: Deeds and agreements
topics.summary: Sale deed, lease deed, gift deed, will and power of attorney.
notes: A sale deed contains parties, recitals of title, consideration, conveyance, covenants and schedule of property.
A will need not be registered but must be attested by two witnesses.
A power of attorney authorises an agent; one relating to immovable property is usually registered.
outcomes: Draft a sale deed and a will

courses.title: Human Rights Law, LLB Semester 6
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public KSLU syllabus (KSLU CBCS, 2025-26)

topics.title: Human rights: concept and generations
topics.summary: Nature, generations and the international bill of rights.
notes: Human rights are universal, inalienable, indivisible and interdependent.
Generations: civil and political; economic, social and cultural; collective (development, environment).
International Bill of Rights: UDHR (1948), ICCPR and ICESCR (1966).
outcomes: Explain the nature of human rights
Describe the International Bill of Rights

topics.title: UN human rights system
topics.summary: Charter-based and treaty-based bodies.
notes: Human Rights Council and its Universal Periodic Review.
Treaty bodies, e.g. the Human Rights Committee under the ICCPR.
Conventions: CEDAW, CRC, CAT, CRPD.

topics.title: Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
topics.summary: NHRC, SHRCs and human rights courts.
notes: The NHRC inquires into violations and recommends action; its chair is a former Chief Justice of India or Supreme Court judge.
The NHRC cannot inquire into matters more than one year old.
Human rights courts are designated sessions courts.
outcomes: Explain the role of the NHRC

topics.title: Protection of vulnerable groups
topics.summary: Women, children, SC/ST, persons with disabilities and transgender persons.
notes: POCSO Act, 2012 protects children from sexual offences.
SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989; Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.
NALSA (2014) recognised transgender persons; Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019.
outcomes: Identify protective laws for vulnerable groups
